title: Heating on all day, or off while you're out? The math
description:
Your house loses heat in proportion to how much warmer it is inside than outside. With the heating on, a 20 degree gap leaks about 4 kW the whole time you're out: 36 kWh over 9 hours. Switched off, the house drifts down to 15 C, the gap shrinks, and the leak slows to 3 kW. Warming it back up only replaces what leaked out while you were gone: about 31 kWh, so you save about 5 kWh (13% of those 9 hours). The US Department of Energy calls 'reheating costs more' a common misconception, and puts the saving from a daily 8-hour setback at up to 10% a year. (Heat pumps with electric backup heat are the one case to watch: a big jump in the setpoint can switch on the backup heaters, so let them warm up slowly.)

Numbers checked in code (verify.py): Newton's law of cooling for a house with a 0.2 kW per degree heat loss, plus a minute-by-minute thermostat simulation of 100,000 random houses (switching off never used more). Sources: US DOE Energy Saver (thermostats), Energy Vanguard.

Heat loss rate depends on the temperature difference between inside and outside (https://www.energyvanguard.com/blog/do-programmable-thermostats-save-energy/)

US DOE Energy Saver: 'A common misconception associated with thermostats is that a furnace works harder than normal to warm the space back to a comfortable temperature after the thermostat has been set back, resulting in little or no savings'; 'save as much as 10% a year on heating and cooling by simply turning your thermostat back 7-10 F for 8 hours a day' (https://www.energy.gov/energysaver/thermostats, via search excerpt 2026-11-26)

beats.say: Heating on all day, or off while you're out?
You've heard that warming a cold house back up burns more than you saved. It can't.
Say it's 0 degrees outside, your house is at 20, and you're out for 9 hours.
Your house leaks heat through every wall. The bigger the gap between inside and out, the faster it leaks.
Heating on: the gap stays at 20, so it leaks 4 kilowatts. Over 9 hours, that's 36 kilowatt hours, all burned to refill the leak.
beats.caption: Heating on: the gap stays at 20, so it leaks 4 kW. Over 9 hours, that's 36 kWh, all burned to refill the leak.

beats.say: Heating off: your house drifts down to 15. The gap shrinks, so the leak slows to 3.
But tonight, your boiler has to warm the whole house back up. That's the catch, right?
Warming it up only puts back what leaked out. And less leaked: 31, not 36.
A cold house leaks slower, so off always wins. The US Energy Department puts it at up to 10% a year.
So if you're out twice as long, do you save twice as much?
